title: Read-only file system: find which mount is read-only and make it writable
summary: The error means the disk, USB stick or partition that holds this folder is mounted read-only, so nothing can be written there even if your permissions allow it. These steps show which mount is read-only and, when it is safe, how to make it writable again.

steps.explain: Find out which mount holds this folder and whether its options start with ro, which means read-only. Replace <FOLDER> with the folder that refuses writes.

placeholders.name: FOLDER
placeholders.description: The folder where saving or copying fails

steps.expect: One line with the mount point and its options, for example '/ ro,relatime,...'. When the options start with ro, the whole mount is read-only.

steps.explain: List all read-only mounts on the system. A USB stick, a CD or an ISO image, or a disk that the system switched to read-only after errors can show up here. A Docker container started with --read-only also shows ro on /.
steps.expect: Lines with the mount point, file system type and options that include ro. If nothing is printed, no mount is read-only; the problem is then file permissions (Permission denied) instead.

alternatives.explain: Same check by reading the kernel's list of mounts directly.
alternatives.expect: Lines in the same kind of format; a read-only mount has ro in its option list.

steps.explain: Read the kernel log for disk problems. If the system switched a disk to read-only because of errors, the log says so. Needs administrator rights.
steps.expect: Often nothing relevant. Lines with 'I/O error' or 'remounting filesystem read-only' mean the disk itself has a problem; read the warnings before step 4.

steps.explain: Make a read-only disk writable again. This works for disks that were mounted read-only by mistake or switched to read-only by the system. It does not work for CDs, DVDs or ISO images, which are always read-only: copy the files to another place instead.

placeholders.name: MOUNT_POINT
placeholders.description: The mount point from step 1 or step 2, the first column of the output

steps.expect: No output and the prompt comes back. Then step 1 shows rw at the start of the options instead of ro.

verify.expect: writable, when the folder is on a mount that accepts writes. If it still says read-only, the mount is still read-only.

rollback.explain: Undo step 4 if you decide the mount should be read-only again.

placeholders.name: MOUNT_POINT
placeholders.description: The same mount point you used in step 4

warnings: Check step 3 before step 4. If the log shows I/O errors, the disk is probably failing: stop writing to it, copy what you can to another disk, and do not rely on it.
Remounting with rw does not repair the file system. If the system switched the disk to read-only after errors, check it with fsck while it is unmounted.
Do not change read-only system folders such as /usr or /boot to fix an app. A read-only system folder is usually intentional.
